Why Instagram shows “AI info” on your photo — and how to remove the metadata behind it

Posted a real photo and Instagram tagged it with “AI info”? It is usually not the pixels — it is the metadata your editing app wrote into the file. Here is how it works and how to clean it.

Updated 2026-11-07 · 5 min read

What is the “AI info” label?

Meta adds an “AI info” label (formerly “Made with AI”) to posts, Reels and Stories on Instagram, Facebook and Threads when it believes an image was created or modified with AI. Depending on the case it appears under your username or in the post’s menu.

Why does my real photo get the label?

One of the main signals Meta reads is the metadata inside the file, using two industry standards:

  • C2PA / Content Credentials: a signed record that AI generators and some editors embed in the image.
  • IPTC DigitalSourceType in the XMP metadata, with values such as trainedAlgorithmicMedia (fully AI-generated) or compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia (a photo edited with AI).

Editing apps can write these fields as soon as you use a generative feature — for example Generative Fill or Generative Remove in Photoshop or Lightroom, or AI erase tools on some phones. That is why photographers often see the label on genuine photos where AI only removed a small object.

Step 1 — Check what your image contains

  1. Open IA Cleaner → Images & documents.
  2. Drop the exact file you were going to post.
  3. Look for entries marked AI, such as XMP with DigitalSourceType or JUMBF / C2PA Content Credentials.

Step 2 — Remove the metadata and post the clean copy

  1. Click Download to get the cleaned image. It is cleaned losslessly — same pixels, no extra compression.
  2. Upload that cleaned file to Instagram.
  3. Make cleaning the last step: if you open and re-export the image in an editor afterwards, it may write the metadata again.

On a phone, open iacleaner.com in your browser, choose the photo from your gallery, download the clean copy and post that one.

What this can’t guarantee

  • Metadata is one of the signals. Meta also looks for invisible watermarks embedded in the pixels (such as Google’s SynthID), uses its own detection, and applies the label when you turn on “Add AI label” yourself. Removing metadata doesn’t affect those.
  • Meta’s rules ask you to disclose realistic content made or significantly altered with AI, and it may add a label or take action if you don’t. If your image is AI-generated, label it — this tool is for files where the metadata doesn’t reflect what you actually did.
